content_list.content_text: The 1990s saw the return of directors and actors who had made landmark films in the past. Long after his heyday in the 1970s, Robert Altman (1925-2006) reemerged with the excellent The Player (1992) and Short Cuts (1993). The latter's fragmented narrative and huge cast prompted favorable comparisons with another of the director's works, Nashville (1975).

information.contentText: To prepare for their roles in the film, De Niro, Pesci, and Liotta spoke frequently with Pileggi, who shared research material left over from writing the book. According to Pesci, the improvisations came out of rehearsals in which Scorsese gave the actors freedom to do whatever they wanted. The director had transcripts made of these sessions, took the lines he liked best, and put them into a revised script, which the cast worked from during principal photography.

content_list.title: American Beauty (Part 1) - The Art of Character
content_list.description: American Beauty is one of my favorite films, and its fantastic screenplay has so many lessons to learn from. In this video, Michael explains how screenwriter Alan Ball builds and reveals his characters.

movie.overview: Lester Burnham, a depressed suburban father in a mid-life crisis, decides to turn his hectic life around after developing an infatuation with his daughter's attractive friend.
movie.title: American Beauty

content_list.content_text: Terrence Malick (b. 1943), who returned to filmmaking with The Thin Red Line (1998) after a 20-year hiatus, chose to tackle World War II, casting a philosophical eye on the conflict in the Pacific. Among actors, two giants of cinema shared the screen for the first time when Al Pacino (b. 1940) and Robert De Niro (b. 1943) starred in the crime epic Heat (1995).

content_list.title: The Chaos of War with Realism and Intensity
content_list.description:
From his earliest work, Steven Spielberg showed an almost uncanny gift for filmmaking, above all for suspense machinations and special effects, a gift to which audiences responded in droves. But the resounding success of early films such as Jaws (1975) and Close Encounters of the Third Kind (1977) - which helped cement modern Hollywood's blockbuster mentality - somehow hurt Spielberg's reputation. Longing for respect, he knew his films would always be regarded as mere mass entertainment and technical exercises.

Even so, the director tried to broaden his range with mature efforts such as The Color Purple (1985) and Empire of the Sun (1987), but it was only with Schindler's List (1993), the harrowing Holocaust narrative, that he finally produced a film that pleased critics and audiences alike. With the exception of his two high-impact action films, Jurassic Park (1993) and The Lost World: Jurassic Park (1997), Spielberg has remained more or less serious ever since.

Saving Private Ryan introduced something new into the director's vocabulary: a violent, visceral intensity. Spielberg had dealt with violence before, of course, but typically in a cartoonish way or else carefully restrained (and later exploited) as a dramatic counterpoint to punctuate moments of extreme horror. Ryan's opening battle sequence, however, is relentless. As soon as the American boats reach the Normandy beach, young men are torn apart by incessant hails of machine-gun fire, whose bullets pierce their useless helmets with a sickening sound. And it does not end there. Soldiers are blown to pieces. Limbs fly through the air and litter the ground. The sea turns blood red. The camera moves erratically as the film takes on the color of death. The "new" Spielberg takes no prisoners.

It is true that the Spielberg of old cannot always resist the pull of sentimentality. A pair of flimsy bookends opens and closes the film on a purely manipulative note, and Spielberg encourages John Williams, his favorite composer, to indulge his most tear-jerking tendencies. What is even more uncomfortable is that Spielberg uses the same techniques to show the horrors of war not only in his stunning opening battle scene but also in the more traditional good-versus-evil conflict of the film's conclusion.

But the familiar good guy-bad guy dichotomy ends up turning the antiwar message into something more challenging. War is hell, Spielberg acknowledges, except when you are winning, because, in the end, it is victory that confers the right to dictate the rules of morality. Saving Private Ryan contains enough darkness behind the smoke of war to fend off accusations of being blindly patriotic. Looking out over thousands of graves, a soldier asks his wife: "Tell me I'm a good man." It is an ambiguous way of asking not only whether "it was worth it," but also whether it was justified. These are questions that surely stay with all those who survive when the camera stops, revealing the death and destruction all around, even if caused by the noblest of causes.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the text by Joshua Klein, published in the book 1001 Movies You Must See Before You Die

content_list.content_text: De Niro continued his partnership with longtime ally Martin Scorsese (b. 1942) in GoodFellas (1990), which took the director back to the streets of his youth for the first of three films set in New York. Next came The Age of Innocence (1993) and Bringing Out the Dead (1999), but the city's existential angst was better captured by Abel Ferrara (b. 1951): King of New York (1990) and Bad Lieutenant (1992) are two of the greatest and darkest cinematic portrayals of the city.

information.contentText: The genesis of The Truman Show was a screenplay written by Niccol in 1991, inspired by the Twilight Zone episode "Special Service." The original draft had more of the tone of a science fiction thriller, with the story set in New York City. Scott Rudin bought the script and promptly pitched the project to Paramount Pictures. Brian De Palma was interested in directing the film before Weir took over and managed to make it for just 60 million dollars of the estimated 80 million budget. Niccol rewrote the screenplay while the filmmakers waited for Carrey's schedule to free up for shooting. Most of the film was shot in Seaside, a planned community located in the Florida Panhandle.

content_list.title: Good Will Hunting - The Psychology of Character
content_list.description: Good Will Hunting is a film that puts the psychological aspects of story structure right on the surface. This video examines how the characters use defense mechanisms to protect themselves, how supporting characters in a story can be designed to break down those defenses, and how these elements work together to create a powerful catharsis for both the characters and the audience.

movie.overview: Will Hunting has a genius-level IQ but chooses to work as a janitor at MIT. When he solves a difficult graduate-level math problem, his talents are discovered by Professor Gerald Lambeau, who decides to help the misguided youth reach his potential. When Will is arrested for attacking a police officer, Professor Lambeau makes a deal to get leniency for him if he will get treatment from therapist Sean Maguire.
movie.tagline: For the first 20 years of his life, Will Hunting has called the shots. Now he's about to meet his match.
movie.title: Good Will Hunting

content_list.content_text: Spike Lee (b. 1957), one of New York's most famous sons, exposed the demand for films depicting African American life with Jungle Fever (1991), Malcolm X (1992), and Clockers (1995). Mario Van Peebles's (b. 1957) New Jack City (1991) and Menace II Society (1993), by the Hughes brothers (Albert and Allen, b. 1972), reinforced that interest, although lesser directors seemed more interested in glamorizing violence than in focusing on the human drama.

quote.quote: As far back as I can remember, I always wanted to be a gangster.
quote.author: Henry Hill (Ray Liotta) in GoodFellas

content_list.content_text: Combining human drama with violence laced with black humor, Quentin Tarantino (b. 1963) easily earned himself the title of enfant terrible of American cinema. Cleverly crafted works such as Reservoir Dogs (1992), Pulp Fiction (1994), and Jackie Brown (1997) showed that he is a talented, if willful, filmmaker. He also wrote the original screenplay for Natural Born Killers (1994) which, along with Reservoir Dogs, Bad Lieutenant (1992), and Crash (1996), ranks among the most controversial films of the decade.

information.contentText: Tarantino was working at Video Archives, a video rental store in Manhattan Beach, California, and originally planned to shoot the film on 16 mm with a budget of thirty thousand dollars, with producer Lawrence Bender playing Nice Guy Eddie. However, when actor Harvey Keitel became involved with the project, he agreed to act in it and co-produce it. Keitel was then cast as Mr. White. With the actor's help, they were able to raise one and a half million dollars for the film.

content_list.content_text: Among Hollywood dramas aimed at a mass audience, The Truman Show (1998) offered a perfect platform for the dramatic talents of Jim Carrey (b. 1962) and was Peter Weir's (b. 1944) best film since Witness (1985). James Cameron's (b. 1954) Titanic (1997) swept the box office and the Oscars in 1998. However, Cameron's screenplay, the film's weakest element, lost out to Good Will Hunting (1997).

content_list.title: The First Rule of Fight Club
content_list.description:
Fight Club is perhaps the high point of David Fincher's career. Many people will probably read that statement with disdain, preferring to name other films by the director as his best, but in terms of the perfect union of form and substance, performances, blend of special effects, and message, Fight Club is, at the very least, his most thought-provoking and intriguing work. After all, the protagonist is the narrator (Edward Norton), but he has no name, recalling the John Doe of Se7en (1995). He is an ordinary man, designed so that anyone in the audience can identify with him. He suffers from insomnia and can only cure it by having moments of catharsis in support groups for all kinds of diseases and problems. There he meets Marla Singer (Helena Bonham Carter), another faker like him, who, because he sees his own sham in her, sends him back to square one with his insomnia. He is a recall specialist; that is, he determines whether, mathematically, it is worthwhile for the company he works for to recall the cars it manufactures or whether it is better business to let people die. In this back-and-forth across the United States, he meets Tyler Durden on a plane, one of his "single-serving" friends, who makes soap.

Together, they find a new form of catharsis, fighting each other in the middle of the street. Soon this craze draws the attention of others, and Fight Club then takes shape. From there, Durden, with his natural leadership and anarchist ideas, begins to build a veritable cult that goes around committing anti-establishment acts across the country. But Tyler Durden does not exist. He is merely a way the nameless narrator's mind found to escape his unbearable daily routine, his conformity to what society dictates. After all, why would anyone in their right mind need a yin-yang-shaped coffee table, or Italian shoes, or a trendy apartment? And this revelation is cleverly woven into the film and is there for anyone to see, done even more cleverly than M. Night Shyamalan (b. 1970) did - in the same year, mind you! - in The Sixth Sense (1999). Famously, David Fincher embodied the anarchist motto of Chuck Palahniuk's book, which provided the basis for Jim Uhls's (b. 1957) brilliant screenplay, and worked that atmosphere visually. We know something is wrong, but the first time we see the film, we cannot pinpoint what it is and only find out at the end.

But Fight Club is not its ending, just as The Sixth Sense is not either. The film is, in fact, an extremely rich and pleasurable thematic treasure that, in a nutshell, criticizes the status quo. The anarchy the film proposes is liberating, critical, intelligent, profound. It is no joke. What we watch makes us think, makes us look around and realize that having for the sake of having is almost an addiction imposed from the top down. Chances are we do not need - or even truly want - what we have or think we want. Look around you and see if that is not exactly the case.

From the very first frame of his fourth fiction feature, David Fincher handles computer graphics in exemplary fashion. We begin literally inside the Narrator's head and set off on a gigantic flashback recounting how he ended up in that desperate situation, with the barrel of a gun stuck in his mouth. And this perfect fusion of computer and practical effects continues throughout the film, giving the director broad freedom to subvert what we have grown used to expecting from movies. Whether it is the reconstruction of the explosion of the Narrator's apartment or his brief cataclysmic dream on the plane, everything is woven into the work without our noticing when the CGI, supervised by Kevin Tod Haug (b. 1956), kicks in (a Fincher trademark in his work).

In addition, the elegance of Fight Club's production design is impressive. From convincing, distinctive costumes for each character - it is hilarious to watch the deterioration of the Narrator's wardrobe - to haunting sets such as Tyler Durden's "mansion," everything works to shake us out of the torpor we live in and to bring Uhls's fascinating screenplay to life. And the cinematography by Jeff Cronenweth (b. 1962) - son of Jordan Cronenweth (1935-1996), who worked with Fincher on Alien³ (1992) - carries aspects of both Se7en and The Game (1997) over to Fight Club.

Fincher also avoided the obvious with the score and delivered something powerful when he chose the Dust Brothers to create something postmodern, heavy, and representative of the kind of counterculture and anarchy put forward by the original work. The result is exhilarating, with clever music syncing that emphasizes, without overdramatizing, the film's key moments. Last but not least, there is the main trio. Of the three, Bonham Carter stands out the least, since she literally repeats the type of performance we have grown used to seeing from her. That does not mean, however, that she is not good. Still, by comparison, her work pales next to Norton and Pitt who, each in his own way, give memorable performances. The Narrator's transformation from "ordinary man" to leader of Project Mayhem (or second-in-command...) is worthy of a tip of the hat, full of nuances that make his journey perfectly believable. Tyler Durden does not undergo the same degree of transformation, but since his personality only fully emerges in the final third, we can still understand the development of this projection of the Narrator's psyche without finding it strange that the soap salesman we are introduced to on the plane is the same man who blows up entire buildings at the end. Fight Club is a one-of-a-kind experience. An audiovisual triumph that needs to be seen again and again to be appreciated in all its fullness.
content_list.credits: Summary based on the article "Crítica | Clube de Luta" by Ritter Fan in Plano Crítico.

content_list.content_text: Steven Spielberg (b. 1946) balanced popcorn movies such as Jurassic Park (1993) with more serious dramas such as Schindler's List (1993), a powerful account of the Holocaust with an excellent re-creation of the Warsaw ghetto and of life in an extermination camp. The film's documentary style was used again in Saving Private Ryan (1998).

information.contentText: Matt Damon, a former Harvard student, originally intended to make the title character a physics prodigy. He discussed his idea with Sheldon L. Glashow, Nobel laureate in physics and at the time a Harvard professor. Glashow told him the premise did not ring true to him and suggested that the main character be a math prodigy. He referred Damon to his brother-in-law, Daniel Kleitman, a mathematics professor at M.I.T., who provided advice on the story.

content_list.content_text: Besides these veterans, four young directors offered glimpses of brilliant potential. David Fincher (b. 1962) caught the attention of audiences and critics with Fight Club (1999), which, despite being a box office failure, would become a cult classic of the 1990s. Bryan Singer's (b. 1965) The Usual Suspects (1995) led audiences through a provocative maze, thanks to the twisty screenplay by Christopher McQuarrie (b. 1968).

quote.quote: Stern, if this factory ever produces a shell that can actually be fired, I'll be very unhappy.
quote.author: Oskar Schindler (Liam Neeson) in Schindler's List

content_list.content_text: Sam Mendes (b. 1965) burst onto the scene in 1999 with American Beauty (1999), which gave Kevin Spacey (b. 1959) one of the best roles of his career (alongside Frank Underwood in House of Cards) and cast a weary eye on middle age and American domestic life. Boogie Nights (1997), directed with remarkable assurance by Paul Thomas Anderson (b. 1970), re-created the Los Angeles porn scene of the 1970s and 1980s, hinting at the body of work that would make him one of the most original filmmakers of the following decade.
content_list.content_credits: Summary based on the text by Ian Haydn Smith, published in the book "Cinema: The Whole Story" by Philip Kemp

movies.title: Fight Club
movies.overview: A ticking-time-bomb insomniac and a slippery soap salesman channel primal male aggression into a shocking new form of therapy. Their concept catches on, with underground "fight clubs" forming in every town, until an eccentric gets in the way and ignites an out-of-control spiral toward oblivion.

movies.title: American Beauty
movies.overview: Lester Burnham, a depressed suburban father in a mid-life crisis, decides to turn his hectic life around after developing an infatuation with his daughter's attractive friend.

movies.title: Saving Private Ryan
movies.overview: As U.S. troops storm the beaches of Normandy, three brothers lie dead on the battlefield, with a fourth trapped behind enemy lines. Ranger captain John Miller and seven men are tasked with penetrating German-held territory and bringing the boy home.

movies.title: Pulp Fiction
movies.overview: A burger-loving hit man, his philosophical partner, a drug-addled gangster's moll and a washed-up boxer converge in this sprawling, comedic crime caper. Their adventures unfurl in three stories that ingeniously trip back and forth in time.

movies.title: Good Will Hunting
movies.overview: Will Hunting has a genius-level IQ but chooses to work as a janitor at MIT. When he solves a difficult graduate-level math problem, his talents are discovered by Professor Gerald Lambeau, who decides to help the misguided youth reach his potential. When Will is arrested for attacking a police officer, Professor Lambeau makes a deal to get leniency for him if he will get treatment from therapist Sean Maguire.

movies.title: The Truman Show
movies.overview: Truman Burbank is the star of The Truman Show, a 24-hour-a-day reality TV show that broadcasts every aspect of his life without his knowledge. His entire life has been an unending soap opera for consumption by the rest of the world. And everyone he knows, including his wife and his best friend is really an actor, paid to be part of his life.

movies.title: Titanic
movies.overview: 101-year-old Rose DeWitt Bukater tells the story of her life aboard the Titanic, 84 years later. A young Rose boards the ship with her mother and fiancé. Meanwhile, Jack Dawson and Fabrizio De Rossi win third-class tickets aboard the ship. Rose tells the whole story from Titanic's departure through to its death—on its first and last voyage—on April 15, 1912.

movies.title: GoodFellas
movies.overview: The true story of Henry Hill, a half-Irish, half-Sicilian Brooklyn kid who is adopted by neighbourhood gangsters at an early age and climbs the ranks of a Mafia family under the guidance of Jimmy Conway.

movies.title: Boyz n the Hood
movies.overview: Boyz n the Hood is the popular and successful film and social criticism from John Singleton about the conditions in South Central Los Angeles where teenagers are involved in gun fights and drug dealing on a daily basis.

movies.title: Malcolm X
movies.overview: A tribute to the controversial black activist and leader of the struggle for black liberation. He hit bottom during his imprisonment in the '50s, he became a Black Muslim and then a leader in the Nation of Islam. His assassination in 1965 left a legacy of self-determination and racial pride.

movies.title: Schindler's List
movies.overview: The true story of how businessman Oskar Schindler saved over a thousand Jewish lives from the Nazis while they worked as slaves in his factory during World War II.

movies.title: Forrest Gump
movies.overview: A man with a low IQ has accomplished great things in his life and been present during significant historic events—in each case, far exceeding what anyone imagined he could do. But despite all he has achieved, his one true love eludes him.

movies.title: Se7en
movies.overview: Two homicide detectives are on a desperate hunt for a serial killer whose crimes are based on the "seven deadly sins" in this dark and haunting film that takes viewers from the tortured remains of one victim to the next. The seasoned Det. Sommerset researches each sin in an effort to get inside the killer's mind, while his novice partner, Mills, scoffs at his efforts to unravel the case.

movies.title: The Sixth Sense
movies.overview: A psychological thriller about an eight year old boy named Cole Sear who believes he can see into the world of the dead. A child psychologist named Malcolm Crowe comes to Cole to help him deal with his problem, learning that he really can see the ghosts of dead people.

movies.title: The Shawshank Redemption
movies.overview: Framed in the 1940s for the double murder of his wife and her lover, upstanding banker Andy Dufresne begins a new life at the Shawshank prison, where he puts his accounting skills to work for an amoral warden. During his long stretch in prison, Dufresne comes to be admired by the other inmates -- including an older prisoner named Red -- for his integrity and unquenchable sense of hope.

movies.title: Philadelphia
movies.overview: Two competing lawyers join forces to sue a prestigious law firm for AIDS discrimination. As their unlikely friendship develops their courage overcomes the prejudice and corruption of their powerful adversaries.

movies.title: Unforgiven
movies.overview: William Munny is a retired, once-ruthless killer turned gentle widower and hog farmer. To help support his two motherless children, he accepts one last bounty-hunter mission to find the men who brutalized a prostitute. Joined by his former partner and a cocky greenhorn, he takes on a corrupt sheriff.

movies.title: Heat
movies.overview: Obsessive master thief, Neil McCauley leads a top-notch crew on various daring heists throughout Los Angeles while determined detective, Vincent Hanna pursues him without rest. Each man recognizes and respects the ability and the dedication of the other even though they are aware their cat-and-mouse game may end in violence.

movies.title: Mulholland Drive
movies.overview: Blonde Betty Elms has only just arrived in Hollywood to become a movie star when she meets an enigmatic brunette with amnesia. Meanwhile, as the two set off to solve the second woman's identity, filmmaker Adam Kesher runs into ominous trouble while casting his latest project.

content_list.subtitle: The events that shaped the world
content_list.title: Timeline of Events from 1990 to 2009
content_list.description: '90s independent cinema dominates the screens, and animation breaks new ground with Pixar. CGI reaches a new level with The Matrix, and Latin American and European cinemas capture the world's attention. Click here to see a chronological view of the main events in cinema from 1990 to 2009.
